name: Chrysin

lead: Chrysin is a flavone found in honey, propolis and passionflower. Lifters take it as a natural aromatase inhibitor, hoping less testosterone converts to estrogen, giving higher testosterone, more muscle and a leaner physique.

In cell and enzyme experiments chrysin has shown activity against aromatase. Oral absorption is very low, reported at roughly 0.003 to 0.02 percent with rapid excretion, and Wikipedia reports no evidence that oral chrysin inhibits aromatase clinically or affects testosterone. Registered human studies are small pilots on absorption, safety and exercise.

paras: It is sold as a capsule in bodybuilding supplement stacks and is usually combined with other hormone-support products. Users typically take it for several weeks while training and checking bloodwork.

As of 2016, Wikipedia reports no toxicity attributed to chrysin in clinical trials or adverse event reports, while noting nonclinical data that raise possible concerns. In 2016 the FDA did not recommend adding chrysin to the bulk-substances list for compounding.

angle.text: Chrysin is a flavone from passionflower and honey that lifters take hoping to block aromatase, keep more testosterone and look leaner and more muscular. Absorption by mouth is very low, and no human study shows it changes testosterone.

lead: Chrysin (5,7-dihydroxyflavone) is a flavone, a type of flavonoid, found in honey, propolis, passionflowers (Passiflora species), Scutellaria baicalensis and some mushrooms and fruits [1][2]. It is an ingredient in some dietary supplements [1].

It entered bodybuilding and hormone-management supplement culture on the claim that it inhibits aromatase, the enzyme that converts androgens to estrogens, and could therefore raise or protect testosterone. Wikipedia states that oral chrysin has no clinical aromatase-inhibitor activity and that there is no evidence it affects testosterone levels [1]. Its oral bioavailability is reported as very low [1].
A large preclinical literature describes antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and neurological effects in cells and animals [3]. Human clinical data are minimal.
infobox: Sold as a dietary supplement; FDA declined to add it to compounding bulk list in 2016 [1]

paras: Chrysin has the formula C15H10O4, with hydroxyl groups at the 5 and 7 positions of a flavone skeleton [1][2]. It is a yellow crystalline solid with low water solubility [2]. Reported concentrations vary widely between sources, from about 0.1 mg/kg in honeydew honey to far higher amounts in propolis [1].

In binding assays, certain flavonoids and phytoestrogens interact with estrogen receptor beta [4]. Reviews describe chrysin's laboratory activities including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, neuroprotective and anxiolytic effects [3]. Methylated flavonoids were reported in a 2006 study to have greatly improved intestinal absorption and metabolic stability compared with unmethylated ones, which is relevant to chrysin's poor oral availability [5].
Wikipedia cites a peak plasma level of 12 to 64 nM in a 1998 study and notes research into nanoformulations to improve absorption [1].

No published clinical studies of chrysin for testosterone, estrogen or physique outcomes were found. Wikipedia states that as of 2016 there was no clinical use and no evidence that oral chrysin changes testosterone levels [1].

Two small studies are registered: an 18-person completed study of chrysin bioavailability and safety after oral intake, started in December 2024 [6], and a 15-person completed pilot of chrysin and exercise performance, started in January 2025 [7]. Results are not summarised here.

Wikipedia reports that a review (Samarghandian et al., 2017) considers intake of 0.5 to 3 g per day safe, and that no toxicity had been attributed to chrysin in clinical trials or adverse event reports as of 2016, though nonclinical data suggested possible concerns [1]. In 2016 the FDA did not recommend including chrysin on the bulk drug substances list under section 503A [1].

lore.intro: Chrysin appears in bodybuilding supplement culture as an over-the-counter anti-estrogen alternative; no forum sources were available to quote for this article.

claims.claim: Chrysin is a natural aromatase inhibitor that raises testosterone.

timeline.event: Study reports binding of phytoestrogens and flavonoids to estrogen receptor beta [4].
